node.label: J. G. A. Pocock
node.date_label: The Ancient Constitution and the Feudal Law (1957) · The history of political thought: a methodological inquiry (1962) · The Machiavellian Moment (1975) · Concepts and Discourses: A Difference in Culture? (1996) · Barbarism and Religion: volumes 1 and 2 (1999) · Barbarism and Religion: volume 6, Barbarism: Triumph in the West (2015) · John Robertson, John Pocock’s Histories of Historiography (2025)
node.description: A historian of political thought and historiography who reconstructs the languages in which political thinking becomes possible. His methodological inquiry treats thinking as historical activity rather than only as coherent philosophy. The Machiavellian Moment presents a selective inquiry into republican fragility in time. In the 1996 concepts-and-discourses exchange he welcomes conceptual lexicons but questions whether they can reconstruct the complexity of political languages, and criticizes Skinner’s search for the modern state for risking anachronistic categories. John Robertson’s later account follows the historiographical problem from the ancient constitution to the six volumes of Barbarism and Religion; those books remain mediated rather than newly read here.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Ancient Constitution and the Feudal Law (1957, known through bibliography and John Robertson’s account); “The history of political thought: a methodological inquiry” (1962, selected 2009 reprint); The Machiavellian Moment (1975, introduction read in the retained source review); “Concepts and Discourses: A Difference in Culture?” (1996); Barbarism and Religion (six volumes, 1999–2015; dated and discussed through Robertson, 2025). Additional bibliographic selections: Virtue, Commerce, and History (1985 essay collection; earlier component dates remain distinct; collection body unread here). “British History: A Plea for a New Subject” (1975, Journal of Modern History 47(4), 601–621; separate comments by A. J. P. Taylor, Gordon Donaldson and Michael Hechter, 622–626, and Pocock reply, 626–628; issue metadata checked, bodies unread here). Politics, Language and Time (Atheneum first-edition collection, 1971; distinguish Methuen 1972; earlier essays keep their original dates; collection body unread here).
node.scope_note: Fresh reading 2026-10-24: printed pp. 3–4, 9–11 in the 2009 publisher excerpt of the 1962 methodological inquiry; the complete 1996 concepts-and-discourses contribution pp. 47–58; Robertson’s 2025 article pp. 1–4 closely, with later sections/endnotes consulted for the six-volume sequence. The earlier reading of The Machiavellian Moment introduction vii–x is preserved, not represented as a newly read complete book. No body of the 1957 or 1999–2015 books was read. Pocock explicitly cannot read German and discusses the Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe through Richter; the new objections preserve that limit and his praise of complementary inquiry. His private correspondence and late political essays were not read. The 1996 publication is separate from the December 1992 symposium.

incident_edges.relationship: Treats political thinking as historical activity within available languages and distinguishes this inquiry from extracting only systematically coherent philosophy (1962; reformulated 1996).
incident_edges.evidence_note: Selected 1962 reprint pp. 3–4, 9–11 and 1996 pp. 47–50 read. This is an individual contribution within the contextual field, not an exclusive founding claim. The existing collective field-to-intellectual-history arrow, also naming Skinner and Brett, is preserved.

incident_edges.relationship: Asks whether an alphabetical history of concepts can reconstruct the complexity of political languages and avoid projecting the historian’s categories onto earlier actors (published 1996).
incident_edges.evidence_note: Pocock, Concepts and Discourses, pp. 47–55, especially pp. 50–55. He explicitly cannot read German and responds to Richter’s presentation of the lexicon. He welcomes a complementary conceptual history and does not dismiss Koselleck’s project or claim first-hand inspection of all its articles. The distinction is an acknowledged methodological challenge, not an assertion that Cambridge and conceptual history are mutually exclusive schools.

incident_edges.relationship: Singles out Skinner’s search for the modern concept of the state as exposed to the risk of imposing later categories on language users who did not employ those terms (published 1996).
incident_edges.evidence_note: Pocock pp. 54–55 and p. 55 n. 2 explicitly name The Foundations of Modern Political Thought, volume II’s conclusion (1978), and the essay The State. This specific criticism coexists with substantial sympathy for Skinner’s general methodological contention and intellectual collaboration. The cited books/essay were not newly read or independently judged here.

incident_edges.relationship: Answers Pocock’s objections by treating discourse and conceptual history as interdependent and defending alphabetical organization as a way to leave historical transformation open to investigation (published 1996).
incident_edges.evidence_note: Koselleck’s own response pp. 62–66, especially pp. 64–66, read. He accepts the uniqueness of situated speech acts but argues that later reception and reuse make conceptual history necessary. He rejects a general incompatibility of methods; this does not mean that Pocock himself asserted such a simple opposition. This is a qualified methodological answer to specific questions, not a complete rebuttal of Pocock’s scholarship.

incident_edges.relationship: Pagden uses Pocock’s account of political languages as distinguishable language-games to explain how historians reconstruct an argument’s vocabularies, conventions and intelligibility.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Pagden’s own opening discussion explicitly names and uses Pocock’s formulation. The publisher’s substantive opening excerpt was read; the complete 1987 introduction and Pocock’s chapter were not freshly read. This is a particular methodological resource, not influence inferred from the editorship or the whole Cambridge school. The print contribution is 1987; 2009 is the online publication date.

incident_edges.relationship: Bailyn identifies Pocock’s research among the resources used to reconstruct the British opposition traditions in revolutionary American thought.
incident_edges.evidence_note: The foreword reproduced in the 1992 enlarged edition, printed xii, explicitly places Pocock with other British political-thought researchers. Robbins, Gough, Laslett, Weston and other named scholars retain their distinct credit; no sole-source or general Cambridge-school lineage is asserted. The original 1967 copy and Pocock’s cited works were not collated or freshly read.

named_group_routes.relationship: renews study of political argument and action
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Skinner’s interventions and Pocock’s political languages renew political-intellectual questions; their approaches are not identical. Skinner’s selected 1969 pages distinguish causal conditions from intended interventions. Pocock’s methodological excerpt asks about actual levels of thinking, while the 1975 introduction selects republican fragility and a proposed Atlantic continuation; the latter’s full transmission argument is not independently verified here.

named_group_routes.relationship: Skinner explicitly credits the Investigations in asking about historical language use
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Interview answer 6 recalls reading and discussing the work, connecting it to purposeful discourse and public intentions. This retrospective evidence concerns Skinner’s pre-2000 practice; it does not establish one philosophy shared by Pocock or all contextual historians. The 1969 article p. 37 directly cites Investigations §§43 and 79, adding contemporary primary evidence to the retrospective interview. Endpoint review 2026-10-24: the retained statement names this promoted individual; only its endpoint is repaired. Prior sources, wording and reading qualifications remain. See the individual entry and research packet for the fresh reading scope.

named_group_routes.relationship: Canada and the British World: imperial history from the settler colonies
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Buckner (1993, abstract) argues that historians of the second British Empire neglect the colonies of settlement and Pocock's "Greater Britain", and that historians of the settler colonies share the blame; Canada and the British World (2006) surveys Canadian history "through a British lens" while eschewing nostalgia. The atlas has no separate imperial-history entry; nationaltradition (national and imperial narratives) is the nearest. Comparison, scoped to the British World strand.

named_group_routes.relationship: Makes the historically possible intervention, rather than a timeless doctrine, central to interpreting political texts; recalls that public uses and intentions guided his practice (1969; retrospective interview 2002).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: 1969 pp. 37–38, 50–52 and 2002 answers 1/6 reread, with the earlier wider reading scope retained. This is his individual methodological contribution to the contextual field. The reception arrows for Wittgenstein and Collingwood keep their old IDs; aggregate edges also naming Dunn, Pocock and Brett are not reassigned to him.

verification.note: Official institutional full PDF. Preface pp. 5–6, Richter pp. 7–9, Pocock pp. 47–58 and Koselleck pp. 59–66 read closely; final reply pp. 67–70 consulted for concluding context. Copyright/preface date the publication to 1996; the preface dates the symposium to December 1992. Claims are dated to the published text, not assumed identical to an uncollated oral delivery. Pocock explicitly says he does not read German and responds through Richter’s presentation. His criticism of the lexicon and his particular criticism of Skinner coexist with openness to complementary methods. Koselleck argues for interdependence, not an opposition between two homogeneous schools. Other contributions and original German lexicon entries unread, except as stated. No new direct quotations.

verification.note: Complete answers to questions 1 and 6 read in 33-page unpaginated manuscript. Journal issue independently corroborates 2002, pp. 34–63, DOI 10.7227/R.6.1.4. Explicit retrospective reception of Collingwood’s changing questions and question/answer method, alongside analytical philosophy; opening cautions against tidy self-narration. No complete interview or 1969 article collation. His Austin/Collingwood biographical speculation is not evidence of transmission. Retrospective testimony concerns pre-2000 practice. Answer 6 also explicitly recalls reading the Investigations and Austin’s How To Do Things with Words, connecting these to public use and historical interventions; those passages reread for revision 1.47. This is selective first-person reception, not a common method of all contextual historians.
